article_title: Fostering Self-Directed Growth with Generative AI: Toward a New Learning Analytics Framework
citation: Qianrun Mao. (2024). Fostering Self-Directed Growth with Generative AI: Toward a New Learning Analytics Framework. https://www.google.com/search?q=Fostering+Self-Directed+Growth+with+Generative+AI+Toward+a+New+Learning+Analytics+Framework
title: A2PL framework: three foundational pillars (Capacity to Aspire, Complex Thinking, Self-Assessment) reconfigured around Self-Directed Growth
description: The Aspire to Potentials for Learners framework reconfigures the three foundational pillars of SDL summarized by Morris (2019): "The Capacity to Aspire represents the core essence of humanistic philosophy; Complex Thinking serves as the foundation of constructivist epistemology; and Self-Assessment embodies the principles of pragmatic philosophy". At the center is Self-Directed Growth, and together the pillars represent a learning process that is individual, purposeful, and developmental. The framework aligns summative self-assessment with the two layers of Capacity to Aspire within and across learning cycles.
requirements: Summative self-assessment must be combined with Capacity to Aspire to drive an ongoing, iterative, and sustainable SDL process
constraints: The article states detailed technical implementations, platform engineering, and algorithmic design fall outside its scope and are reserved for future research
target_learners: learners in non-synchronous online learning environments

article_title: Fostering Self-Directed Growth with Generative AI: Toward a New Learning Analytics Framework
citation: Qianrun Mao. (2024). Fostering Self-Directed Growth with Generative AI: Toward a New Learning Analytics Framework. https://www.google.com/search?q=Fostering+Self-Directed+Growth+with+Generative+AI+Toward+a+New+Learning+Analytics+Framework
title: A2PL three-level intervention design: Person, Task, and Person x Task levels
description: The A2PL intervention operates at three levels. At the Person level, learners reflect on aspirations and long-term vision of societal achievement and professional growth. At the Task level, "Learners and GAI co-create complex thinking tasks within real world scenarios that align with learners' aspirations". At the Person x Task level, learners construct a summative self-assessment framework by aligning identified ability, skill, and strategy gaps with task-aligned personal aims, fostering a more clearly defined strategic learning pathway. Starting from the second round, reflective practices adjust alignment and initiate a new SDL cycle.
requirements: GAI must refrain from disclosing that the assessment pertains directly to SDL, so learners' frameworks indicate internalized skills rather than prompted responses
constraints: The article states success is contingent on whether learners' summative self-assessment frameworks reflect analytical cognition of SDL into the depth of its procedures and components
target_learners: self-paced learners in non-synchronous online environments
examples: Table 1 maps learning stages to theoretical guidelines, GAI features, and skills developed, including root-cause analysis for systemic thinking and scenario-based tasks for critical thinking and problem-solving

article_title: First graders' literacy and self-regulation gains: The effect of individualizing student instruction
citation: Connor Carol McDonald, Ponitz Claire Cameron, Phillips Beth M., Travis Q. Monét, Glasney Stephanie, Morrison Frederick J. (2010). First graders' literacy and self-regulation gains: The effect of individualizing student instruction. Journal of School Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsp.2010.06.003
title: Assessment-to-instruction (A2i) web-based planning software
description: The Assessment-to-instruction (A2i) software "translates assessment results into specific recommendations for amounts and types of instruction for each student in the classroom". It automatically records teachers' use, including total minutes of active use, which the study used as a metric of planning and a proxy for intervention fidelity. An integral part of the ISI intervention, A2i includes planning-specific components such as the Literacy Minutes Manager and the Group Activity Planner, and is available at http://isi.fcrr.org.
requirements: Teachers must be trained to use the software to plan individualized instruction, and assessment results must be available to generate recommendations
constraints: A2i use minutes are a proxy for fidelity, not a direct measure of instructional quality; treatment teachers' use ranged widely, from 15 to 370 minutes
target_learning_goals: Individualized literacy instruction matched to students' vocabulary and reading skills
examples: Treatment teachers used A2i on average about 160 minutes from September through May; the ISI Treatment variable coded control teachers as 0 and treatment teachers by their A2i minutes

article_title: ASK-IT/A2L: Assessing student knowlede with instructional technology
citation: Dufresne, R. J., Gerace, W. J., Mestre, J. P., & Leonard, W. J. (2000). ASKIT / A2L: Assessing Student Knowledge with Instructional Technology. UMPERG Technical Report PERG-2000#09-SEP#1-28pp. https://www.umass.edu/umperg/
title: Twelve habits of mind for students in a question-driven physics classroom
description: The ASKIT/A2L project identifies twelve good habits of mind — natural tendencies or willingnesses applied to mental processes — that students should develop to cope with a question-driven, interactive physics classroom. The report breaks "the desirable tendencies of students into six basic and six advanced “habits of mind”", from seeking alternative representations and comparing and contrasting to generating multiple solutions and meta-communicating. Teachers target these habits when designing and choosing items.
requirements: Teachers must encourage the habits during activities and experiences, and students need opportunities to commit to answers, explain reasoning, and learn from mistakes.
constraints: The report states the advanced habits of mind are "more easily applied to later stages of learning".
examples: Basic habits include seek alternative representations, compare and contrast, explain/describe/draw, predict & observe, extend the context, and monitor and refine communication; advanced habits include generate multiple solutions, categorize and classify, discuss/summarize/model, plan/justify/strategize, reflect/evaluate, and meta-communicate.
key_sources: Dufresne, R. J., Gerace, W. J., Mestre, J. P., & Leonard, W. J. (2000). ASKIT / A2L: Assessing Student Knowledge with Instructional Technology. UMPERG Technical Report PERG-2000#09-SEP#1-28pp. https://www.umass.edu/umperg/

article_title: ASK-IT/A2L: Assessing student knowlede with instructional technology
citation: Dufresne, R. J., Gerace, W. J., Mestre, J. P., & Leonard, W. J. (2000). ASKIT / A2L: Assessing Student Knowledge with Instructional Technology. UMPERG Technical Report PERG-2000#09-SEP#1-28pp. https://www.umass.edu/umperg/
title: Five stages of cognitive development as intermediate goals for physics instruction
description: The report recommends substituting cognitive goals for short-term or long-term problem-solving goals. These goals break "the development of knowledge and skills into five stages, all of which are needed for expert-like problem solving": explore/define/hone concepts; link and cluster concepts, operations, and procedures; develop analysis and reasoning skills; develop concept-based problem-solving skills; and organize, prioritize, and structure knowledge. Only one stage refers specifically to problem solving.
requirements: Teachers monitor student progress through the stages, and all the cognitive skills should be targeted from the very beginning of the course.
constraints: Students do not need to fully understand concepts before moving to the next stage; the report warns that spending too much time in the first stage will actually inhibit students' intellectual growth.
examples: The stages can be applied to individual topics such as kinematics, interactions, Newton's laws, and conservation of momentum, and to subtopics such as force, acceleration, or kinetic energy.

article_title: ASK-IT/A2L: Assessing student knowlede with instructional technology
citation: Dufresne, R. J., Gerace, W. J., Mestre, J. P., & Leonard, W. J. (2000). ASKIT / A2L: Assessing Student Knowledge with Instructional Technology. UMPERG Technical Report PERG-2000#09-SEP#1-28pp. https://www.umass.edu/umperg/
title: Model-based design paradigm for creating instructional items
description: The model-based design paradigm is the project's procedure for developing items. It starts from findings of cognitive research — alternative conceptions, expert–novice differences, cognitive overload, hierarchical analysis — and three premises, including that "Proficient problem solving requires structured knowledge". From a cognitive framework it derives concept-based problem solving, then uses "a “web” or “matrix” of cognitive goals and habits of mind to create instructional materials" for the project's materials, producing items that shift instruction toward beneficial mental processes.
requirements: Development starts from cognitive research findings and the three stated premises about cognition and problem-solving proficiency.
constraints: The report states "There is no cookbook for developing items"; practice, testing, observation, and reflection are the most useful guide, and copying superficial features of successful items is the most common pitfall.
examples: For each cognitive goal, the developers create items to encourage one or more habits of mind, used across MindsOn Physics, ASKIT, and Assessing-to-Learn Physics.
key_sources: Dufresne, R. J., Gerace, W. J., Mestre, J. P., & Leonard, W. J. (2000). ASKIT / A2L: Assessing Student Knowledge with Instructional Technology. UMPERG Technical Report PERG-2000#09-SEP#1-28pp. https://www.umass.edu/umperg/

article_title: ASK-IT/A2L: Assessing student knowlede with instructional technology
citation: Dufresne, R. J., Gerace, W. J., Mestre, J. P., & Leonard, W. J. (2000). ASKIT / A2L: Assessing Student Knowledge with Instructional Technology. UMPERG Technical Report PERG-2000#09-SEP#1-28pp. https://www.umass.edu/umperg/
title: Question cycle: a lesson structure of six phases built around formative assessment items
description: The question cycle is the report's recommended structure for a class period organized around formative assessment items. The typical class period can be "broken down into two or three cycles of six phases": present an item, let students work individually or in groups, collect answers, show histogram, discuss as a class, and wrap-up. The cycle asks a question first, and discussion and wrap-up are shortened or lengthened to fit students' answers.
requirements: Items should vary in style, difficulty, and purpose, and it is usually best if most of the questions yield a range of responses to stimulate class-wide discussion.
constraints: The cycle "does not need to be followed strictly at all times"; it is a good starting point, especially for teachers new to conducting an interactive classroom.
examples: In the discuss phase the teacher keeps discussion student-directed; wrap-up may be a short lecture, what-if questions, or re-presenting the same item and showing a new histogram.
key_sources: Dufresne, R. J., Gerace, W. J., Mestre, J. P., & Leonard, W. J. (2000). ASKIT / A2L: Assessing Student Knowledge with Instructional Technology. UMPERG Technical Report PERG-2000#09-SEP#1-28pp. https://www.umass.edu/umperg/

citation: Dufresne, R. J., Gerace, W. J., Mestre, J. P., & Leonard, W. J. (2000). ASKIT / A2L: Assessing Student Knowledge with Instructional Technology. UMPERG Technical Report PERG-2000#09-SEP#1-28pp. https://www.umass.edu/umperg/
title: ASKIT/A2L classroom communication system
description: The classroom communication system is the technology component of the ASKIT/A2L approach. It is used "to monitor individual or group progress on an item, collect students’ answers, compile and sort the answers into histograms, display the histograms, and store responses for possible retrieval at a later time". The report also credits it with time management, enforcing instructor-set time limits for submissions, and notes students generally enjoy using it.
requirements: Students need an input device for submitting answers, and the system enforces the instructor-set time limit for answer submission.
constraints: Without technology, duplication is difficult but not impossible; flash cards are not anonymous and promote a teacher-centered approach because only the teacher sees all the cards.
examples: Monitoring which groups are ahead of or lagging behind the rest lets the teacher target help to struggling groups before the class-wide discussion.
